worked_example: Take TCJA full extension. Against pre-2025 law it adds about $4.6 trillion to the deficit, because the individual cuts would otherwise expire after 2025. Against current law the same proposal scores $0: P.L. 119-21 already made those cuts permanent, so scoring the extension again would double-count. The 2026 debate is the same shape on a new yardstick — whether to extend the *temporary* pieces of that law, which current law still assumes expire.

laws.title: Current law (CBO February 2026)
laws.summary: CBO's February 2026 baseline, which already includes P.L. 119-21.
laws.lesson: A score is the difference from this baseline, not a property of the policy on its own. CBO's February 2026 Outlook already includes P.L. 119-21, so extending the TCJA individual cuts — the 2024–25 debate — is already current law. Scoring that extension again here would count it twice. The live 2026 question is whether to extend the law's temporary pieces (tips, overtime, the $40,000 SALT cap, and others), which this baseline assumes expire on schedule.

laws.title: Pre-2025 law (TCJA/IRA expire)
laws.summary: Current law as it stood before P.L. 119-21: TCJA individual provisions and many IRA energy credits expire on their old schedule.
laws.lesson: Against this yardstick the TCJA individual cuts expire after 2025, as they were written before P.L. 119-21. Extending them is a large new cost — CBO scored a full extension around $4.6 trillion — because the baseline does not already contain it. That is why the same proposal that scores $0 against current law scores trillions here. Other proposals on this page still show the number computed on CBO's February 2026 baseline; a full re-score on January 2025 current law is not in this release, and those rows say so.

versus_current.convention: unified deficit including macroeconomic effects and debt service
versus_current.note: Primary deficits +$3.7 trillion and debt service +$0.9 trillion over FY2026–2035, from the July 2025 cost estimate shifted onto this window; macroeconomic effects take the total to +$4.7 trillion. The conventional $3.4 trillion in publication 61570 is the same law on FY2025–2034 without those two channels.

laws.title: Current law, P.L. 119-21 temporary provisions extended
laws.summary: February 2026 current law, but with P.L. 119-21's temporary provisions made permanent — the live 2026 debate.
laws.lesson: Current law assumes P.L. 119-21's temporary provisions expire: no tax on tips, overtime and a larger senior deduction after 2028, the $40,000 SALT cap after 2029, time-limited factory expensing, and several appropriation boosts. Making those permanent is the same kind of question TCJA extension was in 2024–25, on today's yardstick. CRFB, reading CBO's February 2026 baseline, puts the primary-deficit cost at $1.9 trillion through FY2036 — an eleven-year window, and not a CBO table of the enacted package. Preset rows still show scores computed on current law; they have not been re-run on this scenario.

versus_current.convention: primary deficit; excludes debt service and macroeconomic effects
versus_current.source: CRFB, 19 February 2026, off CBO's February 2026 baseline
versus_current.note: CRFB: making temporary P.L. 119-21 provisions permanent adds $1.9 trillion to primary deficits through FY2036, including about $290 billion in FY2036. The site's scored window is FY2026–2035, so the ten-year increment is smaller by that last year and is not separately published. Tax pieces named: tips, overtime and the senior deduction expire after 2028; the $40,000 SALT cap after 2029; factory expensing is similarly time-limited. Spending pieces (defense and immigration appropriations through FY2029) are in the $1.9 trillion too.
